cases.title: Punjab + Haryana, India
cases.question: India reported that farm fires fell 93% between 2021 and 2025. Is that the whole story?
cases.do: Monitor after 4 pm, add a geostationary feed to fire alerts, and report the early-afternoon count alongside the timing shift.
cases.lesson: A drop in satellite counts can partly be burning moving to hours the satellites don’t see.
cases.sentence: Fire activity here fell about 80% (2021–2025, Oct–Nov), but part of that drop is burning that moved to hours the satellites don’t see.

cases.title: Punjab + Haryana, India
cases.question: Does the same place show the same timing problem in its other burning season?
cases.do: Use the record as it is for this season, with the range shown.
cases.lesson: The check doesn’t say “timing matters” everywhere: this is the built-in control.
cases.sentence: No clear change between 2019 and 2025: the range runs from −38% to +45%. Satellite timing isn’t the issue here.

cases.title: Kalimantan, Indonesia
cases.question: 2019 was an extreme fire year. How far have fires fallen since, and can MODIS answer that?
cases.do: Use the combined record, not a Terra or Aqua series, to report the decline.
cases.lesson: The error can run the opposite way from Punjab: MODIS can exaggerate a decline.
cases.verdict_label: The older MODIS record is off here
cases.sentence: Fire activity fell about 69% (2019–2025, Aug–Sep). Burning hours look unchanged, but a record built from the older MODIS satellites would be off here because their pass times drifted.

cases.title: Cerrado / MATOPIBA, Brazil
cases.question: Did savanna clearing fires fall between 2019 and 2025?
cases.do: After 2020, use the combined record rather than MODIS, and look at the whole series, not two years.
cases.lesson: Satellite drift can bend a MODIS record even when burning hours haven’t changed.
cases.verdict_label: The older MODIS record is off here
cases.sentence: Fire activity changed −21% (2019–2025, Aug–Sep), but the range includes no change. Burning hours look unchanged, but a record built from the older MODIS satellites would be off here because their pass times drifted.

cases.title: California, USA
cases.question: Were California’s 2025 wildfires worse than 2019’s?
cases.do: Compare the whole series, not two years: wildfire years swing too much for a two-year headline.
cases.lesson: Sometimes satellite timing isn’t the issue at all, and Burn Clock says so.
cases.sentence: No clear change between 2019 and 2025: the range runs from −75% to +507%. Satellite timing isn’t the issue here.

cases.title: Paraná Delta, Argentina
cases.question: Did burning in the delta wetlands change between 2019 and 2025?
cases.do: Treat any two-year change here as unverified; there are too few fires for a timing verdict.
cases.lesson: When the data can’t support a verdict, Burn Clock says “can’t tell”.
cases.sentence: Fire activity changed +14% (2019–2025, Jul–Sep), but the range includes no change. There are too few fires here to test whether satellite timing matters.
